title: The first way (ST I.2.3)
hookLine: change needs a source that isn't itself changed

cards: A pot of water sits on the stove. Cold. It could be hot; it just isn't yet.
Then the burner catches, and slowly the could-be becomes is. Small bubbles, then a rolling boil. The water didn't heat itself.
Something already hot had to do it. That's almost too plain to say. But Thomas Aquinas builds his first argument for God on exactly that.
In the Summa he calls it the more obvious way, because it starts from something nobody can miss: things change. Today's word is that first way.

teach.b: First, a word: motion. For Thomas it means any change, a could-be becoming an is. Cold water getting hot.
A seed becoming a tree. Second, the rule.
Nothing gets from could-be to is on its own; it needs something that already is. Thomas's example is fire: fire, actually hot, makes wood, which could be hot, actually hot.
And the same thing can't be giving and receiving the same heat at once. So whatever is changed is changed by another. Third, the chain.
Thomas pictures a hand moving a staff, and the staff moving something else. The staff moves only because the hand moves it.
Suppose every link were like the staff, only passing along motion it got elsewhere, with no source anywhere. Then nothing would move at all. A thousand sticks and no hand push nothing.
So, Thomas says, we must come to a first mover, moved by no other, and this everyone understands to be God.

teach.h: A CHAIN NOW, NOT A FIRST PUSH.
teach.b: Thomas isn't walking back through time to a first push at the start of the world. Later in the Summa he says reason alone can't prove the world had a beginning; that is held by faith.
His example points to a chain right now, like hand and staff. And unmoved doesn't mean frozen, like a statue. It means God has no could-be left; nothing in God is waiting to become.

teach.h: NO CHANGE, NOR SHADOW OF ALTERATION.
teach.b: The letter of James says it, in the Douay-Rheims: the Father of lights, "with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration."

how: Catholic philosophy courses often begin Thomas's five ways with the argument from motion, reading his hand-and-staff chain as what moves things now, not a first moment in time.

s: for Thomas, motion means only moving from place to place

games.q: a hand moves a staff, and the staff moves a stone. the staff only moves because the hand moves it. what does Thomas say about a chain like this?
o: each link could move itself if it tried.
it can run on forever with no source at all.
it has to rest on a first mover, moved by no other.
games.why: with no first mover, no link would move at all: sticks with no hand push nothing. Thomas says this first mover everyone understands to be God.

practice: Find one moving thing, a curtain in a version, steam from a cup, your own chest rising and falling, and watch it without naming anything.
Then ask what's moving it, and what's moving that, one link back at a time, each one leaning on something else.
If you pray, rest at the end of the chain with the one Thomas calls the first mover; if you don't, just keep watching it move.

wordCard.voice: The first way. Thomas's argument from change: whatever changes is changed by another, and the chain must rest on a first mover, moved by nothing.

orig.note: Latin: the first mover — Thomas's phrase in the first way, a first mover moved by no other.

carryVoice: Your line: the unmoved mover. Not a push long ago, but a source right now. Until tomorrow.
